ECE 6390

BPSK decisions and Gaussian error tails

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows how a synchronized binary receiver counts the chance that noise crosses its decision threshold.

A coherent receiver aligns the carrier phase and samples the matched-filter output. In the simple BPSK model the transmitted coordinate is +A or −A, and the observation is y = s + n. Noise n is Gaussian with mean zero and standard deviation σ in the same amplitude units. Equal prior probabilities and equal error costs place the optimum threshold at zero.

Both error events matter: Pb = p₊P(y < τ | +A) + p₋P(y > τ | −A). At equal priors and τ = 0, symmetry reduces this to Q(A/σ). The Q function is the standard Gaussian upper-tail probability: Q(x) = ∫ₓ∞ exp(−u²/2)du/√(2π) = ½erfc(x/√2). BER is dimensionless; multiplying by bit rate gives an expected error count per second.

In a unit-energy signal basis, A = √Eb and σ² = N₀/2, giving coherent uncoded BPSK Pb = Q(√(2 Eb/N₀)). Convert a dB energy ratio to linear form before taking the square root. This model assumes perfect synchronization, Gaussian noise and no residual intersymbol interference.

The adjustable threshold shows why a biased threshold trades one conditional error against the other. With bit-one prior p₊, equal costs and common variance, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) threshold is τ = σ² ln((1−p₊)/p₊)/(2 A). The figure keeps the selected threshold separate from that optimum; unequal priors change which mistakes are more frequent.

Example

At Eb/N₀ = 0 dB, the linear ratio is 1 and Pb = Q(√2) = 0.07865. At 10 dB, Pb = Q(√20) ≈ 3.87×10⁻⁶. For equally likely bits, vanishing signal amplitude approaches Pb = ½.

Practice

1. Why do both transmitted symbols contribute the same conditional error probability at a zero threshold?

Reflect the Gaussian density around zero.

The +A and −A densities are mirror images with the same variance. Their tails beyond the opposite side of zero have equal area; the equal prior weights then sum to one.

2. If ones become more frequent, which direction should the equal-cost threshold move?

A more frequent +A symbol needs less observation evidence to select it.

It moves negative. With p₊>½, ln((1−p₊)/p₊) is negative, making +A the decision over a larger observation region.
